sentences.text: Neovenator was a mid-sized, lightly built carcharodontosaurid dinosaur.
The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — measured approximately 7 to 7.5 meters in length, though one possibly referable specimen suggests a size of 10 meters.
It was likely around 7 meters long and weighed 1 metric ton, with a suggested hip height of about 2 meters.
Teeth associated with the type specimen possess characteristic enamel wrinkles but differ in their precise pattern from other carcharodontosaur teeth.
The first bones of Neovenator were discovered in the summer of 1978 following a storm-induced collapse at Grange Chine.
The genus Neovenator was named in 1996 by Steve Hutt, David Martill, and Michael Barker, with the only known species being N. salerii, named after the Salero family who owned the discovery site.
Bite marks on a Mantellisaurus fossil suggest Neovenator preyed on this iguanodontid dinosaur.
Because Neovenator was terrestrial, researchers assume its sensory organs were used for sensing pressure, temperature, and controlling jaw pressure rather than finding food in water.
Researchers hypothesize Neovenator may have used sensory organs for courtship and sensing nest conditions.
A position within the clade Carcharodontosauria was first suggested in 1998 and supported by comparative morphology and phylogenetic analyses.
In 2010, Neovenator was assigned to its own family, Neovenatoridae.

Researchers suggested in 1996 that Neovenator was closely related to Allosaurus and possibly a member of the family Allosauridae, and a 2000 phylogenetic analysis by Thomas R. Holtz Jr. recovered Neovenator as the sister taxon to Allosaurus.
Neovenator lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago.

Definite remains are from the Barremian-age Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, an environment that was a floodplain intersected by river and lake deposits, while teeth from the Berriasian-age Angeac-Charente bone bed in France may also belong to the genus.

The taxonomic position of Neovenator remains a subject of debate, with Fernando Novas et al. (2013) placing Neovenator at the base of Carcharodontosauridae in a polytomy with Eocarcharia and Concavenator.
Additionally, researchers suggest that the snout of Neovenator was highly vascularized or innervated.
